content: Buruli ulcer is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, a bacterium belonging to the same family as those responsible for tuberculosis and leprosy. The infection initially manifests as painless swelling, which later progresses to the development of skin lesions. As the disease advances, the bacterium produces toxins that suppress the immune system and cause extensive destruction of the skin, underlying tissues, and even bone, leading to severe deformities. The disease predominantly affects the limbs. The first description of Buruli ulcer dates back to 1948, originating from the Bairnsdale district in southeastern Australia. Pathophysiologically, Buruli ulcer is caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, which leads to painless swelling and subsequent skin lesions as the infection progresses. The diagnosis of Buruli ulcer is typically based on the characteristic appearance of the ulcer in regions where the disease is endemic. In cases where the diagnosis is uncertain, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting the IS2404 sequence can be utilized, although this method is not specific to M. ulcerans. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain has a sensitivity of 40–80%, while culture methods have a sensitivity of 20–60%. Antibiotics currently play a limited role in the treatment of Buruli ulcer. Recommended drugs include rifampin, streptomycin, and dapsone. The primary treatment for Buruli ulcer is surgical excision of the lesion. If performed early, this can often be a minor procedure with a high success rate. However, advanced cases may require prolonged treatment, including extensive skin grafting. Surgical intervention can be challenging and is often unavailable in resource-limited settings, particularly in affected regions of the developing world.
